title: Method of moments (electromagnetics)
text:
Development of boundary element method and other similar methods for different engineering applications is associated with the advent of digital computing in the 1960s.[1] Prior to this, variational methods were applied to engineering problems at microwave frequencies by the time of World War II.[2] While Julian Schwinger and Nathan Marcuvitz have respectively compiled these works into lecture notes and textbooks,[3,4] Victor Rumsey has formulated these methods into the "reaction concept" in 1954.[5] The concept was later shown to be equivalent to the Galerkin method.[2] In the late 1950s, an early version of the method of moments was introduced by Yuen Lo at a course on mathematical methods in electromagnetic theory at University of Illinois.[6]

In the 1960s, early research work on the method was published by Kenneth Mei, Jean van Bladel[7] and Jack Richmond.[8] In the same decade, the systematic theory for the method of moments in electromagnetics was largely formalized by Roger Harrington.[9] While the term "the method of moments" was coined earlier by Leonid Kantorovich and Gleb Akilov for analogous numerical applications,[10] Harrington has adapted the term for the electromagnetic formulation.[2] Harrington published the seminal textbook Field Computation by Moment Methods on the moment method in 1968.[9] The development of the method and its indications in radar and antenna engineering attracted interest; MoM research was subsequently supported by the United States government. The method was further popularized by the introduction of generalized antenna modeling codes such as Numerical Electromagnetics Code, which was released into public domain by the United States government in the late 1980s.[11] In the 1990s, introduction of fast multipole and multilevel fast multipole methods enabled efficient MoM solutions to problems with millions of unknowns.[12,13]

Being one of the most common simulation techniques in RF and microwave engineering, the method of moments forms the basis of many commercial design software such as FEKO. Many non-commercial and public domain codes of different sophistications are also available. In addition to its use in electrical engineering, the method of moments has been applied to light scattering[14] and plasmonic problems.[15,16,17]
